input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Review prior approaches to long-form generation, structured prompting, citation-aware generation, and document planning. Contrast linear prompting baselines and citation verification techniques, emphasizing gaps addressed by a graph-aware approach.

output:
This section situates our graph-aware prompting workflow within four strands of prior work: long-form neural text generation, structured or schema-guided prompting, citation- and evidence-aware generation, and document planning and scheduling. Because no external excerpts were provided for this draft, the statements below are presented as concise general background knowledge and do not cite specific papers; we will add detailed, cited comparisons in a revised draft once targeted literature is retrieved.

- Long-form neural generation: Prior research has explored model and prompt designs that aim to preserve global coherence and factuality when producing multi-paragraph or multi-section outputs (general background knowledge). Important challenges include maintaining topical structure and avoiding unsupported assertions across long contexts.

- Structured prompting and schema constraints: Work in structured or constrained generation has investigated the use of templates, intermediate representations, and output schemas to improve controllability and downstream parsing of model outputs (general background knowledge). Such approaches motivate our use of a strict JSON schema for section outputs.

- Citation- and evidence-aware generation: A complementary body of work focuses on integrating external evidence and explicit citations into generated text, and on post-hoc verification to detect hallucinated claims (general background knowledge). These efforts underscore the need for provenance-aware retrieval and conservative citation policies, which we adopt as design principles.

- Document planning and section-level scheduling: Research on document planning and hierarchical generation considers how to decompose a manuscript into interdependent units and schedule generation to improve coherence (general background knowledge). The idea of leaf-first or dependency-aware scheduling informs our section-graph approach.

Limitations of this draft: because no retrieved excerpts were supplied, we do not provide citation-level comparisons or empirical contrasts with specific linear prompting baselines or verification systems here. In the final paper we will (1) cite representative literature for each category above, (2) explicitly contrast our graph-guided, JSON-constrained pipeline with linear prompting baselines and automated citation-checking tools, and (3) highlight empirical differences grounded in the cited sources.
